_: THE settings vocabulary, once. SettingsView.jsx draws its knobs from this file and the assistant (settings_schema.py, appfacts.py) reads the same one, so a knob cannot be called one thing on the page and another in the chat. `groups` is the order the page stacks its sections in; each knob carries group, label, type (switch | number | select | text | brain | brains | channels | timezone | sound | flags), options for a select, desc (one line) and help (the long explanation the page shows).
_panel_owned: Keys a CARD on the page already owns, so the knob list must not also offer them as a bare box. Every aidefaults.SLOTS key and its model_setting belongs here - tests/test_settings_schema.py fails if one is missing, which is what `assistant_ai` (d3bde8bd) and then `judge_ai` both did: a real setting with no KNOB_META entry falls through to the empty 'Other' group as an unlabelled text box, which is the one place nobody would look for it.

kb_semantic.label: Semantic search
kb_semantic.desc: Find documents by meaning, not only by their words: "time off" finds the leave policy.
kb_semantic.help:
Off (the default): the knowledge base is searched by keywords, exactly as before, and nothing extra is installed or run.

On: each passage is turned into a vector by a small embedding model as it is indexed, and a search merges the nearest passages with the keyword hits. Needs an embedding model served at the address below (Ollama by default: `ollama pull nomic-embed-text`). Passages indexed before you switched this on are embedded by the next Reindex. If the model is unreachable, search quietly falls back to keywords.

The text of your documents goes to that address to be embedded. The default is this machine; point it at a remote server only if you are content for the documents to go there. `pip install taskuary[semantic]` (numpy) makes the scan faster on a large library.

kb_embed_url.label: Embedding server
kb_embed_url.desc: Address of a server that answers /v1/embeddings (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM).
kb_embed_url.help: Default http://127.0.0.1:11434, Ollama on this machine. Any server speaking the OpenAI embeddings surface works.

kb_embed_model.label: Embedding model
kb_embed_model.desc: The model that turns passages into vectors (default nomic-embed-text).
kb_embed_model.help: Changing it re-embeds the library on the next Reindex; passages embedded with the old model are ignored meanwhile, so results fall back to keywords until then.

kb_semantic_min.label: Least similarity (0-1)
kb_semantic_min.desc: How close a passage must be in meaning to count as a hit.
kb_semantic_min.help: A nearest-neighbour search always has a nearest neighbour, even when nothing is related, so passages below this cosine similarity are dropped. Raise it if unrelated passages turn up; lower it if related ones are missed. Scales differ between models, and the default 0.5 is a starting point, not a measurement for yours.

intent_classify_enabled.label: Intent triage
intent_classify_enabled.desc: Classify every new message: a task to DO, a question to ANSWER, or FYI to file.
intent_classify_enabled.help:
The heart of the funnel. Every inbound message is read (by the AI picked for sorting at the top of this section, guided by SOUL.md) and classified: task = something must be done, so an agent can be dispatched; reply_only = answering IS the work, so a reply is drafted for your approval; fyi = informational, filed with no task and no draft.

Off: every message becomes a task, which turns newsletters into work items. Leave this on unless you are debugging triage itself.

triage_ai.label: Triage brain
triage_ai.desc: Which AI reads and classifies inbound messages.
triage_ai.help:
TWO BRAINS: a small, fast cloud model (Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure OpenAI) classifies each message in under a second for a fraction of a cent, while your CLI agent — the expensive, capable one — is saved for actually working tasks.

ONE BRAIN, TWO GEARS also works well: pick a CLI agent here and set its 'light model' (Docs → Profiles → Manage profiles → Edit) — triage, drafts, summaries and the digest then run on the cheap fast tier (haiku, gemini-flash…) while coding sessions keep the agent's main model. No second API key, one bill.

Left blank, it is your default brain on its light gear (haiku for Claude) - never whichever connector was added first. Obvious automated noise is filtered by cheap heuristics before any AI is called either way.

triage_backup_ai.label: Backup AI connections
triage_backup_ai.desc: Ordered alternatives for triage, reply drafts, summaries, reports, and assistant chat when the chosen AI is unavailable.
triage_backup_ai.help:
Pick more than one. Taskuary tries them in the order shown when the primary brain hits a session or usage limit, is signed out, has no key, or otherwise refuses the call. A fallback uses its own default model; a model name chosen for Claude is never handed to Codex.

This starts blank because crossing from a cloud API to a local CLI can change cost and privacy. Once you name backups, the same chain protects every short/background AI job as well as the non-coding assistant.

playbooks_enabled.label: Use playbooks
playbooks_enabled.desc: Triage matches new mail to your playbooks, and agents may propose new ones.
playbooks_enabled.help: On: triage is shown every playbook that is switched on, a message that is an instance of one becomes a task worked from it, and a finished job that will recur is proposed as a new playbook for your approval. Off: no playbook is matched or proposed; the playbooks themselves stay on Reports → Playbooks, and a single one can be switched off there instead.

email_signature.label: Email signature
email_signature.desc: The block that goes under every email Taskuary writes for you - exactly this, once. Read it from your sent mail, then fix anything.
email_signature.help:
Saved here, it is the only signature on an email: the AI is told not to sign, any sign-off it writes anyway is taken off, and this block goes under the text exactly as you see it. Chat messages (Teams, Slack, WhatsApp) never get it.

Read it from my sent mail finds the closing lines most of your sent mail shares - quoted history is cut first. Blank means no saved signature: drafts then sign the way STYLE.md describes.

reply_channels.label: Draft replies on
reply_channels.desc: Which channels get a drafted reply at all. Switch one off and its questions just file.
reply_channels.help:
A question arriving somewhere you never answer from should not open a reply task whose draft has nowhere to go. Turn a channel off and messages from it still come in and can still become real tasks — they simply never get a draft, and the funnel says so in the row's reason ('replies are off for slack').

One answer for the whole app: triage uses it to decide whether a question becomes a reply task, the agent wrap-up uses it to decide whether to draft at all, and the approval buttons on the task use it to decide whether Approve can actually send. They cannot disagree.

Two rules are not yours to change here: GitHub also needs 'Reply to issue/PR authors' on its own card (a reply there is a PUBLIC comment), and the read-only trackers — Jira, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty and friends — can never carry a reply because Taskuary only reads them.

calendar_enabled.label: Check your calendar when a reply is about time
calendar_enabled.desc: "Tuesday at 1 works for me" is only drafted if Tuesday at 1 is free. Reads the Outlook card's calendars (needs the Calendars.Read application permission) and a Google calendar if its OAuth fields are on the Gmail card.
calendar_enabled.help:
When the thread mentions a day, a time, a meeting or availability, the responder fetches your busy slots for the next 14 days and is told: never offer a busy time; if the asked time is busy, say so and offer the nearest free one; if the calendar could not be read, say you will confirm. The task gets a note that the calendar was checked.

Agents can read the same thing: POST /api/tools/run with type "calendar".

concierge_ai.label: Assistant tab brain
concierge_ai.desc: Which AI speaks on the Assistant tab and in your phone chat, and walks you through the pipe - the Assistant's own brain. auto = your default coding agent, on its faster, lighter model.
concierge_ai.help:
THREE DEFAULTS, side by side in How mail is sorted: the triage brain, the default coding CLI, and this one.

A CLI agent here can ACT - read a task or message, rerun a report, run a data tool - because it has a shell; it runs in its own scratch folder on a light model (Claude: haiku, Codex: low effort, Gemini: flash, or the agent's own 'light model' from Docs → Profiles) and picks its conversation back up turn to turn, so only the first turn pays the start-up. An API connector answers faster but can only talk. Sending, approving and pushing are your buttons whichever speaks.

concierge_model.label: Assistant tab model
concierge_model.desc: A different model for the Assistant tab, if you want one (e.g. sonnet, or gpt-5.4-mini). Blank = the faster, lighter default. Add @low, @medium or @high to set how hard it thinks, e.g. claude-sonnet-5@medium; a Claude model with nothing added thinks at low.
concierge_model.help: For a CLI this is its --model, and model@effort sets its reasoning effort (Claude --effort, Codex model_reasoning_effort); for an API connector, its model or deployment name. Changing it starts a fresh CLI conversation.

assistant_ai.label: General agent brain
assistant_ai.desc: Which AI works every general task - research, planning, writing, a job with no repository - and answers the floating bubble. Your phone talks to the Assistant, not this.
assistant_ai.help: Normally set on the General agent card at the top of this tab; this row is the fallback if that panel cannot load. A CLI here can run tools, drive a browser and post to the wall; an API connector has no shell, so it can only read and write - quicker, and enough for chat. Blank = the first active API connector, else the default agent.

judge_ai.label: Where runs go
judge_ai.desc: Which AI decides whether a finished report waits under Reports, reaches you right away, or goes out.
judge_ai.help: Normally set on the 'Where runs go' card at the top of this section; this row is the fallback if that panel cannot load. Four yes/nos about a result somebody else wrote, judged against the sentences on the report's own card - it never has to write anything, so a decision model belongs here and a chat model is wasted on it. Blank = the brain that writes each report judges its own run.

draft_ai.label: Drafting brain
draft_ai.desc: Which AI writes the replies and messages you approve, and their subject lines. Blank = the triage brain, as before.
draft_ai.help: Normally set on the Drafting card at the top of this section; this row is the fallback if that panel cannot load. Every reply used to be written by the triage brain, which wants your cheapest, quickest model; a reply in your voice is worth a better one. Nothing is sent without your press, whichever writes it.

draft_model.label: Drafting model
draft_model.desc: A different model for drafting, if you want one. Blank = the drafting brain's own light model, as before.
draft_model.help: For an API connector this is its model or deployment name; for a CLI, its --model, and model@effort sets how hard it thinks.

ai_route_mode.label: Which AI does each job

optionLabels.auto: Auto - by how hard the work is

ai_route_mode.desc: Fixed runs every job exactly as its card says. Auto picks a quick, standard or strong model by the job and how hard triage judged the work.
ai_route_mode.help: Normally set on the line above the AI cards; this row is the fallback if that panel cannot load. In Auto each card is its job's standard model, and the rules under it say when the quick gear or the strong model runs instead - each shown as a sentence with its own switch. A brain whose strong model box is blank never steps up. An explicit pick - yours, a report's, a workflow's - always wins, and nothing is sent without your press either way.

ai_route_strong_cap.label: Strong calls a day
ai_route_strong_cap.desc: At most this many calls a day on a strong model, in Auto. Blank = no cap.
ai_route_strong_cap.help: Normally set on the line under the rules; this row is the fallback if that panel cannot load. Past the cap, work that would step up runs on the standard model and its route says why, and an unsure answer is not asked again. The count is of today's strong routes in the route log, so you can see what used it.

assistant_model.label: General agent model
assistant_model.desc: Override the model for the brain above. Blank = the provider's own default.
assistant_model.help: For an API connector this is its model or deployment name; for a CLI it is the profile's light model. Changing it starts a fresh CLI conversation.

assistant_max_lines.label: Lines per post, at most
assistant_max_lines.desc: The Advisor checks in every 30 minutes and on startup (the 'Advisor' report on the Reports tab — edit its prompt for what it watches for, change the cadence, delete it to turn it off) and posts only when it has something to say. How it SPEAKS is COUNSEL.md in Settings → Docs: edit that to change its voice, how bold it is, what it takes a position on. This caps how much one post says. 5 by default.
assistant_max_lines.help: One AI call per post, and none when there is nothing new. Every line has a key and a state, so it never says the same thing twice. Talk back under a suggestion to correct it or ask a follow-up; the answer and your correction stay with the idea and inform later checks. 'Follow up' drafts the chase in your voice onto the task — nothing is sent by itself; 'Make it a task' starts the agent. Voice: COUNSEL.md (Settings → Docs); what to watch for: the report's prompt. Without an AI connector the facts still post, in the hub's own words. 'Run now' on the Reports tab's Assistant row posts regardless of the schedule.

assistant_followup_hours.label: Silence before a follow-up
assistant_followup_hours.desc: Hours after your last reply on a thread — one that asked for or promised something — before 'no answer yet, follow up?' appears. 24 by default.
assistant_followup_hours.help: Only your own last word counts, and only when it asked or promised something ('could you send', 'by Friday', a question mark). A plain thanks that goes unanswered is not a follow-up. The chase itself is drafted only when you click.

assistant_cold_days.label: Quiet days before a task has 'gone cold'
assistant_cold_days.desc: Open work with no comment, message or run for this many days gets a line. 3 by default.
assistant_cold_days.help: A task with a live agent on it is never cold. One with a draft waiting on the task is named as waiting on you.

slipped_default_days.label: Days of silence before a thread has slipped
slipped_default_days.desc: A thread you wrote on, or a step somebody owes, is 'slipped' - first on your rail, with Chase, Let it go, They answered elsewhere and Remind me - once it has been quiet this many days. For a person the outcome ledger has seen answer three times, their own usual day is used instead. 5 by default.
slipped_default_days.help: Someone whose auto-reply says they are away never slips. The day is read from the ledger, never from the mail.

advisor_events.label: Advise on the item that changed
advisor_events.desc: When an agent stops or asks, a reply arrives, a pull request opens, a task closes, a day is missed or a report lands, the Advisor runs one small prompt on the light model and leaves one line and one verb on that item: the ghost text in the prompt box and the pill where the send arrow sits. On by default.
advisor_events.help: Never a row and never a change to the rail's order: the line attaches to the item and shows when the walk reaches it. The verb is one the item already carries; the number beside it is read from the outcome ledger. Off, the Advisor still runs on its schedule.

advisor_event_cap.label: Event judgements per hour, at most
advisor_event_cap.desc: The small prompt runs once per item per change and never more than this many times an hour; past it, the change is noted as dropped and the item simply has no pill. 30 by default.
advisor_event_cap.help: The Advisor's notes on an item (the clock menu) say when a judgement was dropped for the cap.

assistant_producers.label: What it looks for
assistant_producers.desc: followup = your unanswered asks · promise = what you said you would do and have not · prep = meetings in the next two days, with what came before them · cold = tasks gone quiet · idea = the model's own thoughts from the day's mail, guided by the report's prompt.
assistant_producers.help: Switch a kind off and it never appears in a post again; lines already posted keep their actions and conversation. 'idea' is the only one that needs an AI connector — the others are read straight off the hub's own tables and your calendar. With 'idea' off no model is called at all: the facts post in the hub's own words.

default_brain.label: Default AI for agents
default_brain.desc: Which AI program runs an agent's work when its role does not name one. A role (coding, researcher, analyst) decides the instructions an agent starts with; this decides which program follows them. Blank = each profile's own program.
default_brain.help:
Set from the cards above in normal use — this is the raw value they write. Naming a brain here is what stops a role name being read as a CLI name, which is how TQ-0588's coding work was once routed to Copilot.

A role and a brain are different questions and one name cannot answer both.

backup_brains.label: Fallback AI programs
backup_brains.desc: Tried in order when the first one has used up its allowance, is signed out, or will not start. * = every other one you have set up, in the order they are listed.
backup_brains.help: Failover is for AVAILABILITY failures only — session/usage/rate limits, quota, expired login, a missing executable — never for an agent that simply erred. The task, its messages, attachments, repository and seed prompt all travel to the replacement, which starts a fresh conversation with its own model.

profile_brains.label: A different AI for one role
profile_brains.desc: For a role that should run on a different AI from the default above. Written as JSON, e.g. {"researcher": "codex"}. Blank (the default) means every role uses the default.
profile_brains.help: The escape hatch for 'the analyst should run on codex but everything else on claude'. An unknown role name is ignored rather than guessed at. Edited here because it is rare enough not to earn a picker.

default_agent.label: Default coding CLI
default_agent.desc: The CLI agent that works tasks when nothing names one.
default_agent.help:
Start session, Send to coding agent and auto-dispatch all use this agent unless you pick another in the moment; every agent picker lists it first. The roster itself lives under Docs → Profiles → Manage profiles, where the default row wears the star.

GitHub-specific permissions (may agents open issues? push?) are on the GitHub connector card, because they are decisions about how your team uses GitHub, not about Taskuary.

default_profile.label: Your mail goes to
default_profile.desc: The worker that takes a non-coding task when triage names no specialist for it. Blank leaves it unassigned for you to pick.
default_profile.help:
Set this to the role you do, and the mail you get lands on the worker built for it. An accounts-payable rep picks `ap`: a vendor asking where a payment is becomes a task for the AP worker, which looks it up in the ledger and drafts the answer for you to approve.

Triage still names a specialist when one fits better (a researcher for outside information), and coding tasks always go to the coding agent. Docs → Profiles → Start from a role sets this for you.

general_agent_hands.label: General agents can

optionLabels.cli: do what your CLI agent can

general_agent_hands.desc: What a general (non-coding) agent on a CLI may do. Same as the CLI agent = a shell, files and the connections below, each up to its Authority. Only look things up = read files and search the web, change nothing.
general_agent_hands.help:
A general agent used to be read-only by inheritance from the brain that reads incoming mail - not by a decision (2026-10-05). It now runs with your CLI agent's own permissions, in Taskuary's scratch folder, unless you choose 'only look things up'.

What it may change in your other systems is each connection's Authority, in the table below. Every connection starts at full - what your CLI agent could already do with those credentials - and you narrow the ones you want: at read it can look, and any change becomes a proposal you approve on the task; at write it makes the change itself. A SQL query through a read-level connection is rolled back, whatever it contains.

Mail from someone you do not know never starts an agent by itself - general or coding - so these permissions are only used on work you or a trusted sender started.

repo_trust_private.label: Private GitHub repositories

optionLabels.ours: your own people - a normal agent

repo_trust_private.desc: Who writes pull requests on a private repository. Your own people get an ordinary agent that starts by itself, no prompts.
repo_trust_private.help:
Only people you added can write to a private repository, so its pull requests are your own people's work: they batch together and an ordinary coding agent reviews them, started by itself, with no prompts.

Choose "treat as outside" to give them the same protection as a stranger's pull request on a public repository.

repo_trust_public.label: Public GitHub repositories - who is yours
repo_trust_public.desc: On a public repository anyone can open a pull request. People with write access can push anyway, so trusting their pull requests adds nothing; everyone else's are outside.
repo_trust_public.help:
Trust comes from the role GitHub reports for the author - owner, member or collaborator - which only you can grant and nobody can fake. Having had a pull request merged before does NOT count: one small good change would buy trust for the next.

An outside pull request joins the same task as your own people's and runs with the agent's normal permissions. The triage first reads its text and its diff; one it judges dangerous - a prompt injection, or a change that reaches beyond the project - ranks last, batches apart and is reviewed read-only: everything beyond reading is refused, never asked.

outside_prs.label: Outside pull requests

optionLabels.cloud: review here, fix in GitHub's cloud

outside_prs.desc: What an outside contributor's pull request gets. Fix it in the cloud runs the agent and the tests on a machine GitHub throws away, never yours.
outside_prs.help:
With "fix in GitHub's cloud", an outside pull request that ranking warned about, and whose review asks for changes, is fixed in GitHub's cloud instead of here. It runs a workflow in the repository: one job with a read-only token checks out exactly the reviewed head, runs Claude Code there (tests, builds) and hands back a patch; a second job, which never runs their code, pushes it to taskuary/pr-<number>. Taskuary opens the fix's pull request with your token so your CI runs on it, and Merge merges it with the contributor's commits.

The repository needs the workflow (Taskuary adds it when you press Set up) and one secret, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN - run `claude setup-token` and paste the result under the repository's Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions. The secret sits beside the stranger's code in that throwaway job: it is revocable, and it cannot reach your repository or this machine.

answer_to_agent.label: Hand answers to the working agent
answer_to_agent.desc: An agent asks a question mid-task, Taskuary asks the person, and their reply lands back on the same task. This is what happens next. ask = the task offers one click, 'Type this into the agent's session'. auto = it is typed in the moment it arrives, as if you relayed it. off = it just sits on the task.
answer_to_agent.help:
Only a LIVE session is ever typed into. If the agent already exited nothing happens and the answer simply waits on the task, so `auto` cannot lose anything.

The reason this is a choice rather than always-on: `auto` puts someone else's words into your agent's session without you reading them first. That is usually what you want on your own team's mail and rarely what you want from a stranger's reply, and Taskuary cannot tell the difference well enough to decide for you.

git_flow.label: How finished work lands
git_flow.desc: A draft pull request, or the commits pushed straight onto the default branch.
git_flow.help:
pr (default) = a DRAFT pull request from the task's branch; it merges only when you approve the task's close-out (Merge), or when you merge it on GitHub yourself. direct = the commits already in the checkout are pushed straight onto the default branch — no PR, no review ceremony, which is usually what you want on your own repository.

Direct mode is deliberately narrow: it pushes commits that ALREADY EXIST. A dirty checkout is refused rather than committed for you (Taskuary will not write a commit message over work nobody has read), nothing ahead of the remote is simply 'nothing to do', and a rejected push is reported for you to pull and rebase — it never force-pushes.

Either way 'Agents may push / deploy' on the GitHub card is what allows anything to leave the machine at all, and CI watching follows the work to wherever it landed.

ci_watch.label: Watch CI on the task's pull request
ci_watch.desc: A red build goes back to the agent that wrote the code, with the failing check named.
ci_watch.help:
Once a task has a draft pull request (open it from the task, or let the agent propose one), every sync refreshes its checks.

feedback = a failing build is typed into the live session — 'these checks failed, fix the cause and push again, do not merge' — and recorded on the task; if no session is live the task returns to 'open' so it lands on you. watch = the state is shown on the proof card but nothing is handed back. off (default) = no polling at all.

Each distinct failure reaches the agent ONCE per commit, never on every poll. Taskuary opens drafts; a merge waits for your yes on the task's close-out.

proposals_enabled.label: Agents may propose actions
proposals_enabled.desc: An agent can ASK to open a PR, comment publicly, close an issue or run a tool — each waits for your approval.
proposals_enabled.help:
High-impact actions come off the auto-approve road entirely. Instead of doing them, the agent writes a typed proposal in its transcript (TASKUARY-PROPOSE {"action": "open_pr", …}); when the session wraps up, each valid one becomes a pending review saying what it wants and why. Approving RUNS it; rejecting does nothing.

Every proposal is re-validated at execution, so approving never grants a permission you have switched off — an open_pr proposal still needs 'Agents may push / deploy', a public comment still needs the GitHub card's reply switch. Malformed or unpermitted proposals are refused and recorded on the task rather than dropped silently.

waitroom_drip.label: Tell-the-agent notes land one per stop
waitroom_drip.desc: On: a queue of prompts drips in - each time the agent stops, the next one is typed in, the rest wait their turn. Off: everything queued goes in as one batch.
waitroom_drip.help: The waiting room is a funnel: paste twenty prompts and each becomes its own note, in order. With the drip on, the agent gets one at a time with its full attention - it is told how many wait behind it and that the next comes when it stops again, so it never goes looking. Turn it off to hand over the whole list in one message instead.

coding_auto_enabled.label: Auto-start the coding agent
coding_auto_enabled.desc: Every new coding task immediately opens a live CLI session in its repository. Off: the task waits on the Board for you to send it.
coding_auto_enabled.help:
On: the moment triage says 'this is work' your CLI opens in the task's repository (picked from the SOUL.md repo map) with the full ask seeded: visible on the Board, watchable, interruptible. General work uses the separate assistant auto-start switch. Only plain questions (a reply is drafted instead) and notices (filed) stay out of it. Off: tasks queue as 'needs you' and you start the agent from the task yourself.

A first-time sender from outside your domains never starts an agent by itself - the task lands, you press the button. Requires the CLI installed and signed in on this machine. Nothing ships or sends without your approval either way.

general_auto_enabled.label: Auto-start the assistant on general tasks
general_auto_enabled.desc: Every new general task (research, a question to think through, a job with no keyboard) opens its own assistant session with the ask already put. Off: the task waits for you to open it.
general_auto_enabled.help: Both worker kinds start by themselves by default; each has its own switch. The same holds apply to both: a first-time sender waits for your click (release it from the task), a coding job whose repository is unclear waits for your choice, and a missing AI provider is said on the task instead of failing quietly. A hold never hides the task - it is still triaged and on the Board.

trust_own_domain.label: Who may start a worker without you
your own domains
trust_own_domain.help: Every connected mailbox's domain, plus the owner address in Settings. Public mail domains such as gmail.com or outlook.com never count - everyone has one - so only your own address on them does.

trust_sent_history.label: people you have written to
trust_sent_history.help: Verified Sent Items evidence: this mailbox has sent that exact address something before.

trust_non_email.label: people you talk with in chats
trust_non_email.help: Someone you have talked with one-to-one in that chat app, answered there, or vouched for - not everyone in a group you joined. In Slack, Telegram, Discord and the chat servers Taskuary cannot see your own lines, so there it is only the people you vouched for. Off, only your own words count.

trust_own_domain.desc: An inbound message can open a task AND start the agent on it unattended. These are the three rules that allow it; a sender matching none of them still gets triaged and lands on the Board, and only the unattended start waits for your click.
trust_own_domain.help:
Three separate switches until 2026-09-16, which meant reading all three to know the answer to one question.

your own domains — every connected mailbox's domain and the owner address.

people you have written to — checked in your own records first, then asked of the mail server once per address and remembered. Earlier INCOMING mail is never evidence: a stranger's second message is still a stranger's. A lookup that fails is not proof either way, so the task says so and waits.

people you talk with in chats — someone you have answered in a one-to-one chat, or vouched for by releasing or trusting their task. A group chat is not a room of people you trust. Taskuary sees your own lines in Teams, WhatsApp and iMessage; in Slack, Telegram, Discord and the chat servers it cannot, so there trust comes only from vouching.

Turn all three off and nothing ever starts by itself; every task waits on the Board for you. Turning them off does not stop triage, drafting or filing - only the unattended start.

agent_context_file.label: Write the agent a context file
agent_context_file.desc: Each session gets ~/.taskuary/context/TQ-xxxx.md: this sender's recent mail and what you last wrote them, the topic elsewhere, your calendar, the assistant's read, the learned profile, the whole thread - and the reports of closed tasks on the same sender, subject or repo. The seed says 'read it first'.
agent_context_file.help: The seed prompt is one command line (Windows caps it at 32,767 characters, and when it overflows the ask is what gets cut), so the two-line read rides in the prompt and the rest lives in this file. It is written under Taskuary's own home, never inside a checkout - a stray file in a shared checkout gets staged. Off: the seed carries what it always did and no file is written.

agent_hooks.label: Write Claude Code hooks into your checkouts
agent_hooks.desc: Taskuary adds four hook entries to .claude/settings.local.json in each repository a session opens, so the Board reads the agent's real tool calls instead of guessing from the screen. Switch it off to leave your checkouts untouched — the Board then falls back to reading the terminal.
agent_hooks.help:
The decision here is whether Taskuary may WRITE to your repositories, not whether the Board should be accurate — it should, which is why this ships on.

The file is the project-LOCAL settings Claude itself gitignores, so nothing is committed. Existing hooks are kept and only Taskuary's own entries (marked by the /api/hooks/claude endpoint) are replaced. Removing them by hand is safe; they are rewritten the next time a session opens.

CLAUDE CODE ONLY. The hook format is Claude's, so on codex, copilot, qwen, devin or any other CLI this switch does nothing at all — those sessions are read from the terminal whatever it says.

agent_self_close.label: Let a finished agent close its own task
agent_self_close.desc: An agent that says it has finished wraps itself up: the report is written from its transcript and the reply to whoever asked is drafted for your approval. A session you opened yourself is yours to complete.
agent_self_close.help:
Done was a button, which meant a task finished at 2am produced no report and the person who asked heard nothing until somebody opened the tab. The agent knows it has finished long before you look, so it says so.

Every session is told about one command in its prompt: taskuary --done with one sentence. That closes the task, files the report from what is on screen, and drafts the reply - which still waits for YOUR approval before it leaves. A session that merely stops talking never closes anything.

One exception, and the task decides it: when you start or continue a session on a task yourself, the task is marked stay:open. There the command is refused - the agent's sentence is filed on the task and you mark it done.

Off: the Done button, exactly as before.

auto_sessions.label: Agents at once
auto_sessions.desc: How many unattended agent sessions may run together. The rest queue.
auto_sessions.help:
The one number that decides how much work this machine takes on at once. Four is the default because four live CLI sessions in four checkouts is about what a laptop stays responsive under — each one is a real process with a real model behind it.

Past the limit nothing is dropped: a dispatched task joins the queue and starts the moment a session ends, and the Board shows it waiting with the reason. The Board's floor view is drawn to this number, so raising it widens the room instead of crowding it.

Raise it if the machine has headroom and your tasks rarely touch the same files; lower it to one if you would rather watch a single agent at a time. Sessions you start yourself are never blocked by this.

hand_sound.label: Sound when an agent raises its hand
hand_sound.desc: A session that stops at its prompt, or asks you a question, plays this - from any tab. Off silences it.
hand_sound.help:
The moment worth a sound: the thing you delegated is now waiting on you. It fires once, on the transition from working to waiting, never while you already have the task open in front of you. Sounds are synthesised in the browser - nothing to download.

The desktop notification below is separate: it is the browser's own, so it reaches you when Taskuary is behind other windows, and the first time it asks for permission.

hand_desktop.label: Desktop notification when an agent raises its hand
hand_desktop.desc: The browser's notification, so it reaches you when Taskuary is behind other windows. Click it to jump to the task.

phone_assistant.label: Chat with the assistant in WhatsApp or Telegram
phone_assistant.desc: The default for a channel that has never been asked. Each channel above answers for itself once you set it.
phone_assistant.help:
Name the Assistant chat on the WhatsApp or Telegram card under Connections first. Taskuary then listens only to messages you send in that exact private chat. Other people, other chats and groups cannot command it. This is separate from the Notifications role, so the Assistant chat is not subscribed to ordinary Taskuary alerts.

It is the SAME walk the Assistant tab runs, on the same conversation and the same pipe: the item on the table stays where it was, a reply you ask for is drafted, and a yes sends it. The choices arrive as a poll on WhatsApp and as buttons on Telegram; typing a choice's number works on both.

This switch is the standing permission. The Assistant tab's own "in WhatsApp" button hands the walk over for a session whether or not it is on; the tab keeps working beside it.

The chat only ever answers you: Taskuary writes to it only while you are talking to it there (your last message within 30 minutes, until you say stop) - never a reminder, a follow-up or a summary on its own, and not an urgent item either unless you turn on "Text me urgent items even when I haven't written".

Because answers can contain private workspace information, use a chat only you can read — WhatsApp's Message yourself, or your own private chat with the Telegram bot. Off (default) leaves your messages ignored as before.

phone_urgent_unasked.label: Text me urgent items even when I haven't written
phone_urgent_unasked.desc: Off (default): the Assistant chat stays quiet until you write to it, however urgent something is. On: urgent items may reach it anyway.
phone_urgent_unasked.help:
Taskuary writes to your own WhatsApp or Telegram chat only while you are talking to it there. Off (the default), that holds for urgent items too: they are shaded on the desktop and wait there.

On: an urgent item may reach the chat even when you have not written - a move on a task marked urgent, an urgent by-the-way while the walk is handed to the chat, and a report's alert aimed at your own chat. Nothing else changes: reminders, follow-ups, the morning line and summaries still wait until you write. Replies to other people are not affected by this switch.

phone_walk_channel.label: Which chat the Assistant tab offers
phone_walk_channel.desc: The "Walk me through them in ..." button on the Assistant tab: WhatsApp, Telegram, or both.
phone_walk_channel.help: both (default) = a button for each chat that is connected and has an Assistant chat named. whatsapp or telegram = only that one. A chat is offered only once its card under Connections names an Assistant chat, so choosing Telegram before setting it up shows no button until you do.

phone_morning_line.label: A morning line in the chat
phone_morning_line.desc: Once a day, the assistant's chat says what is waiting and offers the two ways in: walk me through my tasks, set up a report.
phone_morning_line.help:
Off by default: the chat says nothing until you write to it or press Walk me through them. On: the first check after 6:00 sends one line to the Assistant chat on every channel that has one - the count in the pipe and how many are on you, then the two scripts as numbered options, so one reply starts the walk there. Quiet on a day the pipe is empty; never twice in a day.

Even on, it goes only into a conversation you started there in the last 30 minutes: the chat never speaks first.

vision_enabled.label: AI reads attached images
vision_enabled.desc: Screenshots go to the triage AI — "see below" mail is read, not guessed at.
vision_enabled.help:
Half of "see below" mail says nothing in its body: the screenshot IS the request. On: attached images (PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP, up to 4 per message, 5MB each) ride along into triage when the model has vision, and coding sessions get the local file paths to open themselves.

Off: only text is ever sent to the AI — the setting to use if your model lacks vision or images must never leave the machine. The panel still displays attachments either way.

report_images_enabled.label: Charts on reports
report_images_enabled.desc: Reports hand back a bar chart alongside the spreadsheet.
report_images_enabled.help: A report's rows always come back as an .xlsx; with this on they also become an .svg bar chart drawn in the panel — and the summarizing model, which just read every row, picks which column to plot (better than a heuristic grabbing the id column). Off: spreadsheet only.

poll_minutes.label: Background sync (minutes)
poll_minutes.desc: How often the app checks your connections while it is open. 0 turns it off.
poll_minutes.help:
The server keeps this clock, so it runs whichever tab you are on and whether or not you are looking at the app - it is also what makes a SCHEDULED REPORT fire on time, since reports are checked on the same pass.

It used to live in the Timeline tab instead: the countdown died the moment you opened Board or Tasks, restarted itself every time you changed a filter, and with the window closed nothing polled at all - so a report set for 8am Monday only ran if somebody happened to be sitting on the Timeline at 8am on Monday.

10 is the default. Lower it if you want mail sooner and do not mind the API calls; 0 turns recurring background polling off. Sync now, startup catch-up, and an action that must refresh chat context can still fetch.

Chat connectors (Teams, Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, iMessage, Discord) also have a separate recurring fast clock - every 30 seconds unless their card says otherwise. 0 here disables both recurring clocks; manual Sync now, startup catch-up, and action-time refreshes remain available.

startup_sync_days.label: Catch-up window (days)
startup_sync_days.desc: How far back the app reaches when it opens, for what arrived while it was closed.
startup_sync_days.help:
Taskuary is a window you open, not a service — at 5:30am it is closed, so 'anything since I last polled' misses the weekend. On startup every trigger connection is asked for this many days; the window only ever WIDENS (a source last polled a month ago is not pulled forward), and duplicates are never re-ingested.

The daily DIGEST.md synthesis runs right after it. 0 = plain incremental poll on startup.

share_links_lan.label: Share links on your network
share_links_lan.desc: Share on a result can make a read-only link to it that people on your network open in their browser.
share_links_lan.hover: Opens the Share port below to your network - Windows may ask once whether to allow it through its firewall
share_links_lan.help:
Off (the default): no shared link exists and nothing listens for one. On: a second, separate server starts on the Share port below and serves ONE kind of page - a link's frozen copy of one result - to your network. Taskuary itself, and everything behind it, stays on this computer only.

Share -> Shared link takes a frozen copy of that one result and gives it an unguessable address on that port, copied for you to paste. Whoever has the link sees that copy and nothing else of Taskuary - no other result, no task, no setting - and the copy does not change when the result does.

A link expires after 7 days, and Revoke below ends it at once. Turning this off closes the port and every link while it is off. Anyone on your network who is given a link can open it, so share links to results you would email to the same people.

The first time the port opens, Windows may ask whether to let Taskuary through its firewall - allow it on private networks for others to reach the link.

share_port.label: Share port
share_port.desc: The port share links are served on, separate from Taskuary's own. Blank = 7797.
share_port.help: Only the shared pages are served on this port; Taskuary's own port stays on this computer. Change it if another program already uses 7797 - links made before the change stop working, because they name the old port.

mark_read_enabled.label: Handled mail, at the source

optionLabels.archive: mark it read, and move handled mail to Archive

mark_read_enabled.desc: What Taskuary does to a message in your real mailbox: nothing, mark it read once the funnel took it in, or that and move it to Archive once it is handled here.
mark_read_enabled.help:
Leave it (default): Taskuary is a pure reader — your inbox still shows every message bold, so nothing about your mailbox changes because you connected it. Mark it read: anything the funnel ingests is marked read at the source, so the bold rows left over are exactly the ones the hub never saw.

Move handled mail to Archive: everything 'mark it read' does, and once a mail is HANDLED here — its task closed, or its row put down with Handled — it leaves your Inbox for Archive, so the Inbox holds only what is still owed. Outlook moves it to its own Archive folder (Mail.ReadWrite), Gmail takes the Inbox label off (All Mail), and another IMAP mailbox uses its Archive folder when it has one; with none, the mail stays where it is. Mail you handled before choosing this is left alone, and mail nobody has handled is never moved.

WHERE IT APPLIES: Outlook mail (needs the Mail.ReadWrite consent), Gmail/IMAP mailboxes (the \Seen flag), Slack channels (the read cursor moves to the newest line taken), Teams (Graph marks the whole CHAT read — there is no per-message read state there) and WhatsApp (blue ticks, via the bridge).

WHERE IT CANNOT: Telegram and Discord bots have no read state to set, and the trackers — Jira, Linear, GitHub, Sentry and friends — have nothing to mark. This setting is simply a no-op for them.

Marking always runs AFTER the message is safely stored and is best-effort: a refused permission is logged and never costs you the ingest.

timezone.label: Timezone
timezone.desc: The zone the app's clock speaks. Blank = this machine's local time.
timezone.help:
Timestamps are stored in the server machine's local time. Name that zone here and every displayed time wears its label (2:44 PM EDT) — and a browser opened from another timezone still reads the stamps correctly instead of silently reinterpreting them in its own zone.

Use an IANA name (America/New_York, Europe/London, Asia/Jerusalem). Takes effect on the next page load.

timeline_fade.label: Fade bottom of Timeline
timeline_fade.desc: How tall the soft fade is at the bottom edge of the Timeline viewport.
timeline_fade.help: Rows are never dimmed because they are old. A row only gets lighter while it passes through the bottom edge, then returns to full contrast as you scroll it upward. Gentle, normal, and sharp change the height of that band; off removes it. Purely visual - nothing is hidden or removed.

concierge_fast.label: Fast mode

optionLabels.auto: on for Codex, off for Claude

concierge_fast.desc: Runs the Assistant's CLI on its provider's fast tier: Codex's fast service tier, Claude Code's fast mode. By default on for Codex and off for Claude.
concierge_fast.help: Claude bills fast mode as extra usage, outside your subscription, and runs it only when extra usage is turned on in your Claude account; Codex spends your plan's credits faster. Coding and general agents are not changed.

funnel_hours.label: The pipe reaches back (hours)
funnel_hours.desc: How far back ordinary mail, reports and fyi enter the pipe the assistant walks you through. Drafts waiting for your yes and agents waiting on you always enter.
funnel_hours.help: A first launch must not surface a year of never-triaged mail. Twelve hours is a working day; set it to 48 after a long weekend.

funnel_max.label: The pipe holds at most
funnel_max.desc: How many items the pipe shows at once. The rest wait their turn and slide in as you clear it.
funnel_max.help: Order is kept: an agent waiting on you or a draft for your yes is never the one held back.

meeting_grace_minutes.label: A meeting stays on the rail after it starts (minutes)
meeting_grace_minutes.desc: How long a meeting that has started stays on the work rail. 5 by default.

rail_hide_noise.label: Hide auto-replies and answered threads
rail_hide_noise.desc: Keeps withdrawn messages, out-of-office auto-replies and threads where yours is the last word off the work rail. On by default.

fyi_batch.label: FYI read together
fyi_batch.desc: How many fyi the assistant puts in front of you at once. 1 to 10; four by default.
fyi_batch.help: An fyi needs no action, so they come in a batch rather than one at a time. At 1 they arrive singly, which is the slow read-everything walk; at 10 you clear the noise in one card. Anything outside 1-10 is clamped - a 0 would take the fyi lane out of the walk entirely.

chat_keep_days.label: Keep past chats (days)
chat_keep_days.desc: Archived assistant chats older than this are removed once a day. Fifteen by default.
chat_keep_days.help: Only the chat transcript goes. What a chat said about a task stays on the task, and memories, rules and correction evidence are never touched.

feed_days.label: Work rail lookback (days)
feed_days.desc: How many days back the Work rail reads. Display only — nothing is deleted.
feed_days.help: Purely the rail's window. Older messages stay in the database, in task histories, and in search.
